1.pericope_label: And David made him houses in the city of David: a place prepared for the ark, and the Levites called to bear it

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the fabric of the palace and its outhouses, raised with the masons and carpenters Hiram had sent, and observes that from the fourth verse the chapter becomes an account of the Levites employed in the business.

Henry hears the admission of the earlier failure, where a good work was undertaken but God not sought after the due order, and insists that it is not enough to do what is good but we must do it well; he notes that the rule about the Kohathites was express and yet David forgot it, so that even those very knowing in the word of God have it not always ready, and draws the lesson that wherever we build for ourselves we must make room for the ark.

Clarke says David should have thought of the Levites sooner, and the breach upon Uzza would have been prevented; Wesley makes the houses apartments for the several wives and children and explains the new tent by the intention to build the temple forthwith, and reads the sons of the fifth verse as those of Amram or Izhar.

Ellicott renders the houses a palace, places the new tent within the palace precincts while the old tabernacle stayed at Gibeon, calls the enunciation of the law a tacit acknowledgment that it had not been observed before, and works the Kohathite descents in detail; Delitzsch quotes Bertheau that the new arrangement expressly admits a cart to have been contrary to the law, and sets the three principal heads against the three sons of Levi.

debates.question: What were the houses David made?

sides.position: a palace, the plural being intensive, rather than fresh quarters for additional wives
a palace of many apartments for his several wives and children
the royal palace with its apartments and the outhouses its officers needed

debates.question: Why was the first attempt a failure?

sides.position: the Levites were not employed, which David knew and had forgotten
the ark was set on a cart instead of borne on shoulders, which the new arrangement tacitly admits was contrary to the law

outliers: Ellicott alone notes that the parallel does not name Jerusalem as the meeting-place, so that only a full representation of the people can be meant.
Henry alone turns the juxtaposition of palace and tent into a rule, that wherever we build for ourselves we must make room for a church in the house.
themes: a palace finished and a tent pitched
carrying on the shoulder against carrying on a cart

7.pericope_label: Of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah: the remaining Kohathite houses and their chiefs

schools.summary: Ellicott traces the three remaining Kohathite houses to Uzziel and Hebron, and reasons from Exodus and from later lists in Chronicles that the sons of Uzziel here must stand for two houses rather than three, the elder line of Mishael having probably become extinct.

debates.question: How many Uzzielite houses are meant?

sides.position: two, perhaps amalgamated into one, since the family of Elzaphan has already been represented and later lists imply only two stocks

outliers: Ellicott alone works this stretch at all, and infers from the order of the names that the elder Uzzielite line may have died out.
themes: a genealogy with one house missing

11.pericope_label: Sanctify yourselves, both ye and your brethren: the due order recovered, and the ark borne on the shoulder

schools.summary: Gill rejects the supplement his own version prints at the thirteenth verse, reading rather that the Levites were not there at the first and not employed as was their business, and supplies from Maimonides the reason shoulders were required rather than a carriage, both for the honour of the ark and lest its structure be damaged.

Clarke explains the mechanics, the staves passing through the rings and resting on the shoulders so that the ark rested on them as a sedan rests on its poles; Wesley ranks Abiathar as high priest and Zadok as second priest.

Ellicott reads the chiefs’ names etymologically as a confession that the Lord is righteous, that he alone is God and that he hears prayer, details the purifications prescribed for worship, takes the solemn title of the ark for a warning that the undertaking is national, and defends the due order at length against the charge that these books care only for the sanctity of institutions; Delitzsch gives the same sense of the thirteenth verse, noting the predicate is wanting but easily supplied and the contracted form unique.

debates.question: What does because ye did it not at the first mean?

sides.position: that on the first occasion it was not they, the heads of the Levitical houses, who carried the ark, but Uzza and Ahio
that they were not there at the first and were not employed as was their business
supplies a verb, that they had not done it at the first, which none of the three who examine the clause accepts

debates.question: Is the sanctity of institutions the leading idea of these books?

sides.position: the charge is reported and answered: the sanctity of a people cannot be secured except in and through divine institutions, and there are positive institutions in Christianity as well as in Mosaism

outliers: Ellicott alone turns the chiefs’ names into a theological confession, finding in Zadok, Abiathar, Shemaiah, Eliel and Amminadab that the Lord is righteous, the bestower of all excellence, alone God, and a Father who hears prayer.
Ellicott alone argues from the due order to a general defence of positive institutions, asking that if the divine authority of the one is abolished, why not the other.
Gill alone supplies the rabbinic reason for the shoulder, the honour of the ark and the danger to its structure.
Ellicott alone notes that the statement about the bearing anticipates the procession described later, such brief summaries being common in Hebrew narrative.
themes: an English supplement all the witnesses refuse
a due order in the spiritual as in the physical world

16.pericope_label: And David spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers: the three choirs, the warders and the trumpets

schools.summary: Gill identifies Heman as Samuel’s grandson and notes that Ben drops from the list, Azaziah seeming to stand in his room.

Clarke calls Heman, Asaph and Ethan the three chief musicians, makes Chenaniah the master singer who gave the key and the time, and canvasses the versions on Alamoth and Sheminith without deciding; Wesley makes Chenaniah moderator of the music, explains the warders’ duty of keeping profane hands off the ark, declines to interpret the two musical terms, and observes that praising God by instruments had not hitherto been in use but was instituted by David under divine direction.

Ellicott refers the participle sounding to the cymbals alone, reads Alamoth as soprano compass and Sheminith as an octave below the tenor, denies on three grounds that Chenaniah had anything to do with the singing, reconstructs the order of the procession, and argues the two warders are not the minstrels of the same names; Delitzsch sorts the three choirs by instrument and holds that the musical terms plainly denote different keys but cannot now be interpreted.

sides.position: master singer or moderator of the music, giving the key, the time and the stops
captain of the Levites in the carriage of the ark, teacher in bearing, since the context, his other appearances and the word itself all point away from music

debates.question: What do Alamoth and Sheminith mean?

sides.position: the mode of maidens, that is soprano compass, and the mode of the eighth, an octave below the tenor
possibly virgins or women singers, or secret things, or an eight-stringed instrument, or the eighth band of musicians
different keys or parts whose certain signification is no longer recoverable

debates.question: Were the two warders the minstrels of the same names?

sides.position: probably not, since the procession puts the minstrels two places ahead of them, one name differs in form and meaning, and names recur too often here for a second Obed-edom to surprise

outliers: Ellicott alone reconstructs the order of the procession from these verses: the three master-singers with two bands of seven, the marshal of the bearers, two warders, and seven priests with trumpets.
Wesley alone states that praising God by musical instruments had not hitherto been in use, and that David instituted it by divine direction and added it to the other ordinances of that dispensation.
Ellicott alone compares Shemiramoth with the Assyrian name behind the classical Semiramis.
themes: a term for soprano and a term for bass
a conductor of bearers mistaken for a conductor of song
warders set before and behind the ark

25.pericope_label: So David and the elders of Israel went to bring up the ark with joy: the sacrifice, the linen robe, and Michal at the lattice

schools.summary: Gill reads the help given the Levites as help to carry the ark cheerfully and without error rather than bodily strength, and takes the king’s linen to mean that, being among the singers, he was dressed as they were.

Henry makes four things of the help: that providence is to be owned even in what falls within our natural powers, that the bearers remembering Uzza were ready to tremble and were helped by having their fears silenced, that they were helped to do it decently and without mistake, and that ministers who bear the vessels of the Lord have special need of such help.

Clarke grounds the sacrifice in gratitude for preservation, identifies the byssus as the beard of a Mediterranean muscle and reports having seen gloves made of it, and refuses the question of Michal here, sending the reader to his note on the parallel; Wesley repeats Henry almost word for word on the help and thinks the ephod mentioned twice because it was unusual for one who was no Levite to wear a Levitical garment.

Ellicott reads the six paces borne without a sign of wrath as the inference that drew out the offerings, works at length the problem of whether this sacrifice and the one in Samuel are the same and concludes they are not different, thinks the Hebrew for clothed a corruption of the word for dancing, and finds the last verse a modernised form of the older text; Delitzsch agrees about the corruption and reports a conjecture about how it arose, but declines to accept it while other discrepancies stand unexplained.

debates.question: Is the sacrifice here the same as the one in Samuel?

sides.position: probably the same, the narrative being generally parallel and the chronicler having perhaps paraphrased the older text to explain it; the proposal that beasts were killed every six paces by priests stationed along the course is called incredible
two distinct sacrifices, one along the route and one at the journey’s end

debates.question: Was David clothed in linen or dancing with all his might?

sides.position: the Hebrew for clothed is an Aramaic word that could easily displace the rare word for dancing, so the text may be a corruption or an intentional alteration
the same explanation is reported and found attractive, the two words differing only in their last two letters, but it is not accepted while other discrepancies stand
the linen is taken at face value, Clarke identifying the material and Gill explaining that the king was dressed as the singers were

outliers: Clarke alone identifies the byssus as probably the beard of a species of muscle found along the Mediterranean, reporting that he had seen gloves made of it, a deep dark yellow inclining to lilac, and that the material is not heard of in Israel before David.
Ellicott alone corrects the master of the song to the chief of the bearing, and reads trumpet for cornet.
Clarke alone declines to discuss Michal at all, referring the whole business to his note on the parallel where it is left to the reader’s determination.
themes: help owned in what human strength could manage
six paces without a sign of wrath
a robe of byssus or a king dancing
a garment unusual on one who was no Levite
